k-1.x_notes: Strengths: clean format, all boards at actual size, correct mathematics. P2 fewest blocks (answers 3, 3, 6; the side-2 hexagon needing 6 is a real challenge). P3 yes/no with blue only is well chosen: it includes the even-area trapezoid that cannot be covered (7 up, 5 down) and the forced star. P4 fewest greens on triangles of side 2-4, and P5 all rhombus tilings of the small hexagons (2 and 3). Weaknesses: the opener asks children to cover nine hexagons and color each one to match. That is mostly low-level busywork, it needs crayons that are not in the materials list, and 'using different blocks each time' is vague. There are only five problems, and nothing goes beyond the 3-tiling shape, so a fast K-1 group could run out of work. A block legend is repeated on every page.
k-1.y_notes: Strengths: six problems, all correct and at actual size. P1 is a yes/no board set with 'say why', mixing an odd-area board, an even-area board that cannot be covered (5 up, 3 down), the chevron, and possible boards. P2 (fewest greens) and P3 (small hexagon tilings) match X. P4 fewest blocks with the chevron included (3, 3, 4; the trapezoid needs 4). P5 is a two-player game, placing blue blocks one at a time where the last placement wins, on five boards. I verified the answers: first, second, first, first, second. It gives K-1 strategic play that stays engaging. P6 asks for all 6 tilings of the 1-2-2 hexagon, a real stretch, with half-scale shapes to draw on. Weaknesses: the K-1 group probably has the non-mathematician parent, and 'say why' and the game's 'sure to win' depend on that adult. Drawing tilings on half-scale shapes is fiddly for kindergartners.
k-1.reason: Both are correct and concrete, but Y gives K-1 more real mathematics and keeps them busier: the strategy game, the 6-tiling enumeration and the chevron boards. X opens with a coloring task that needs crayons and has fewer problems that stretch the children, which is the organizer's known complaint about K-1 pages.

grades-2-3.x_notes: Strengths: correct throughout. P1's boards are all even-area (two impossible by color count, plus the rhombus and the forced star), so the obstruction is the point. P2 fewest greens on triangles of side 2-5. P4 is a well-built hexagon with two black triangles: J and M are unbalanced, and K and L are balanced and I checked both can be covered. P5 asks for the lower-bound proof and the side-10 case. P6 asks for a 16-triangle board needing as many greens as possible; the true maximum is 6, a good open optimization. Weaknesses: P3 (are chevrons allowed alongside blues any help?) is a thin re-covering task with an expected 'no'. P5 is pure written explanation. P2 spills board H onto the next page. Balance is never shown to be insufficient.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Strengths: correct throughout. P1 mixes an odd-area board with an even-area impossible board. P2's boards with holes include a bowtie that has equal up and down counts but still cannot be covered, an important point that balance is not enough, plus a balanced hexagon with holes that I verified can be covered. P3 and P4 cover the fewest-greens triangles, the lower-bound explanation, and the side 10 and 100 cases. P5 is a chevrons-only table that yields 4, 5, 4, 5 against 2, 3, 4, 5 for blues: a surprising pattern that still answers 'never fewer'. P6 asks for a 20-triangle board needing at least 6 greens. P7 is an open rule-finding problem: two greens on the side-2 hexagon; I checked that every one-up, one-down placement can be covered. Weaknesses: 'explain why' is attached to several problems. '10 small triangles along each side' is slightly loose wording. Proving the rule's sufficiency in P7 is beyond third graders, so the adult must accept evidence.
grades-2-3.reason: Both develop kernel 1 soundly, but Y adds the bowtie, which shows balance is not enough, an open rule-finding capstone, and a more revealing chevron comparison. X is solid but more directed, and its chevron problem is thin.

grades-4-5.x_notes: Strengths: an opening rule settles that turned or mirrored coverings count as different. P1 counts the (n,1,1) family (2, 3, 4) and asks for the n=10 case (11 ways). P2 is the 2-2-1 hexagon with 6 tilings. P3 asks for flip distances from pictures; I decoded and checked them: S to T is 8, S to U is 3, U to T is 5. P4 defines chains with a correct example and then gives four letter pairs: two are valid tilings and two are impossible because the chains would collide. This is an excellent exercise of the ribbon-tiling correspondence. P5 counts all 20 tilings, P6 asks what a flip does to the letters, and P7 asks for the proofs that S to T takes at least 8 moves and that round trips are even. Weaknesses: the chain problem is wordy. The flip graph itself is never drawn. Parity appears only at the end, as an explanation.
grades-4-5.y_notes: Strengths: P1 is the 1-2-2 hexagon with 6 tilings, and P2 draws its flip graph and asks for the farthest pair (4 flips), which is the graph exploration named in the outline. P3 gives flip distances that I verified: A to B is 3, C to D is 4, E to F is 8. P4 explores round trips concretely (4 flips without repeating a hexagon; can 5 or 7 work?) before P6 asks for the proof, which is good act-then-explain sequencing. The P5 ribbon definition and example are correct, and P7 and P8 are counting problems (20 and C(6,3)=20). Weaknesses: there is no statement about whether rotated copies count as different. P2 makes children redraw all six coverings. 'Start with any covering' in P4 can strand a child who picks an extreme tiling, which has only one available flip. Nothing in Y matches X's letter-pair construction puzzles.
grades-4-5.reason: Both are strong, correct and well sequenced for kernel 2. X edges ahead with the clear rule on what counts as different, the n=10 generalization and the letter-pair puzzles that make children use ribbons in both directions. Y's flip graph and parity exploration are comparably good.

overall.reason: Both packets are mathematically correct, at actual size and free of filler. Y is clearly better for K-1 (more substance, a well-chosen game, ends later) and somewhat better for grades 2-3 (bowtie, open rule-finding, chevron table). X is only slightly better for 4-5, so overall the organizer should take Y.
